Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: Surat al-Muddaththir was revealed in Makkah.

Ibn Mardawayh related the same from Ibn al-Zubayr, and it will come that the beginning of this surah was the first part of the Qur'an to be revealed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes (mufassirun) said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was first visited by revelation, Jibril came to him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him upon a throne between the heaven and the earth, like a dazzling light. He was terrified and fell unconscious. When he recovered, he entered upon Khadijah and asked for water, which she poured over him, and he said: "Wrap me up, wrap me up!" So they wrapped him in a cloak, and then (Allah) said: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ ﴿Arise and warn﴾.

The meaning of ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ is: O you who have wrapped himself in his garments, i.e., covered himself with them. Its origin is al-mutadaththir, and the letter ta was assimilated into the dal because they are similar in articulation (idgham, assimilation).

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) recited it with assimilation, while Ubayy read al-mutadaththir according to the original form. Al-dithar is what is worn over al-shi'ar, and al-shi'ar is what lies next to the body. Ikrimah said: the meaning is, O you who are wrapped up in prophethood and its burdens.

Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a far-fetched metaphor, because he was not yet a prophet at that time.

﴿Arise and warn﴾: i.e., stand up, and frighten the people of Makkah and warn them of the punishment if they do not submit (to Islam). Or: rise from your bed. Or: rise with resolve and determination. It was also said that warning here means informing them of his prophethood, and it was said it means informing them of tawhid (the Oneness of Allah).

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: stand and pray, and command the prayer.

﴿And your Lord, glorify﴾: i.e., single out your Master, your Owner and the one who sets your affairs right, with magnification (takbir). It means describing Him, glory be to Him, with greatness and majesty, that He is far greater than having any partner, as the disbelievers believe, and far greater than having a consort or a son.

Ibn al-Arabi said: What is meant is the takbir of sanctification and transcendence, by stripping away opposites, rivals and idols, not taking any protector other than Him, not worshipping anyone besides Him, not seeing any act as belonging to anyone other than Him, and no blessing except from Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: The fa' in ﴿so glorify﴾ entered with the sense of a condition (jaza'), as it entered in ﴿so warn﴾.

Ibn Jinni said: It is like your saying: "Zaydan, so strike" meaning "Zayd, strike," so the fa' is superfluous.

﴿And your garments, purify﴾: What is meant by them is the garments that are worn, according to the linguistic meaning. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to purify his garments and keep them safe from impurities (najasat), and to remove whatever impurity had fallen on them. It was also said that what is meant by "garments" is deeds, or the heart, or the soul, or the body, or the family, or the religion, or the character.

Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Abu Razin said: i.e., your deeds, so set them right.

Qatadah said: Purify your soul from sin, and "garments" is an expression for the soul.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: purify your heart. From this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*So bid farewell to my garments, from your garments you shall be stripped*

Ikrimah said: The meaning is: wear them without treachery and without immorality.

He also said: Have you not heard the words of the poet:

*And by the praise of Allah, I have worn no garment of an immoral man, nor do I cover myself with treachery.*

The poet is Ghaylan ibn Salamah al-Thaqafi. An example of using "garments" for the self is the words of Antarah:

*So I pierced with the long spear his garments; the noble man is not forbidden on the spear-point.*

And the words of another:

*The garments of the Banu Awf are pure and clean.*

Al-Hasan and al-Qurazi said: The meaning is: purify your character (akhlaq), because a person's character encompasses his states just as his garments encompass his body. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Yahya is not blamed for bad character, and Yahya is pure of garment, free.*

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: ﴿and your garments, shorten﴾, because shortening the garment keeps it further from impurities when it trails on the ground. Tawus also said this, but the first (view) is preferable because it is the literal meaning.

There is no figurative use of "garments" for something else by way of a relation with a clear indicator that shows it is intended when used absolutely, and there is no disagreement on such a principle, namely taking the literal meaning when a word is used without qualification. In this verse there is evidence for the obligation of purity of garments in the prayer.

﴿And the abomination, abandon﴾: al-rujz in the language means punishment, and it has two readings: with a kasra on the ra' and with a damma. Polytheism and the worship of idols were called rujz because they are the cause of punishment.

The majority read al-rujz with a kasra on the ra'.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Hafs and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a damma.

Mujahid and Ikrimah said: al-rujz is the idols, as in His saying: ﴿So avoid the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. Ibn Zayd also said this.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: al-rijz is sin, and al-hajr means abandonment.

Qatadah said: al-rijz is Isaf and Na'ilah, two idols that were beside the House.

Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi' and al-Kisai said: al-rujz with a damma is the idol, and with a kasra is the punishment.

Al-Suddi said: al-rijz with a damma on the ra' is the threat. The first (view) is preferable.

﴿And do not bestow favour seeking to gain more﴾: The majority read ﴿do not bestow favour﴾ (la tamnun) with the separation of the doubled letters (fakk al-idgham), while al-Hasan, Abu al-Yaman and al-Ashhab al-Uqayli read it with idgham. The majority read ﴿seeking to gain more﴾ (tasta'kthiru) with a damma, on the basis that it is a circumstantial clause (hal): i.e., do not bestow favour while being one who seeks to gain more. It was also said that it is on the basis of the omission of "an" (that), the original being: do not bestow favour that you seek to gain more, and when "an" was omitted, it became marfu'.

Al-Kisai said: When "an" is omitted, the verb takes the damma.

Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read tastakthir with the addition of "an."

Al-Hasan also, and Ibn Abi Ablah, read tastakthir with a jazm (apocopated form), on the basis that it is a substitute (badal) for tamnun, as in His saying: ﴿he will meet a penalty﴾ ﴿it will be multiplied for him﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], and the words of the poet:

*If you come to us, you will visit us at our homes, and find firewood, thick and a blazing fire.*

Or the jazm is because the connected form is treated as the pause form, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*So today I drink, not bearing a sin from Allah, nor a bold intruder.*

with the sukun on "ashrab."

This reading has been objected to, because "tastakthiru" cannot be a substitute for "tamnun," since bestowing favour is other than seeking to gain more, and it cannot be a response to the prohibition (jawab al-nahy).

The predecessors (al-salaf) differed about the meaning of the verse. It was said: The meaning is: do not bestow favour upon your Lord for the burdens of prophethood that you bear, like one who considers what he bears on account of others to be great. It was said: Do not give a gift seeking in it something better than it, as said by Ikrimah and Qatadah.

Al-Dahhak said: This was forbidden by Allah to His Messenger, because he was commanded with the noblest manners and the most sublime character, and He permitted it to his community.

Mujahid said: Do not weaken in seeking to gain more of good, from your saying "a strong rope" when it is weak.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Do not make your deed great in your own eyes by seeking to gain more of good.

Ibn Kaysan said: Do not consider a deed great so that you see it as coming from yourself; rather, your deed is a favour from Allah upon you, since He made a way for you to His worship.

It was also said: Do not bestow favour through prophethood and the Qur'an upon the people, so that you take from them a wage that you consider great.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Do not give your wealth as a means of flattery.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: When you give a gift, give it for your Lord.

﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾: i.e., for the sake of the face of your Lord, be patient in obeying Him and in His obligations. The meaning is: for the sake of your Lord and His reward.

Muqatil and Mujahid said: be patient over harm and denial.

Ibn Zayd said: You have borne a great matter, and the Arabs and non-Arabs will fight you, so be patient over it for Allah's sake.

It was said: be patient under the decrees of destiny for Allah's sake. It was said: be patient over trials. It was said: be patient over the commands and prohibitions.

﴿So when the trumpet is blown﴾: al-naqur is on the pattern fa'ul from al-naqr, as if it is something into which one blows to make a sound. In the speech of the Arabs, al-naqr means sound, and from it is the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*I lower it with a sound when I have raised it.*

They say: "naqara bi-ism al-rajul" when he called the man by name. What is meant here is the blowing into the Trumpet (al-Sur), and what is meant is the second blast, though it was also said the first. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat al-An'am and Surat al-Nahl. The fa' is for causation, as if it were said: be patient over their harm, for before them is a terrifying day in which they will meet the outcome of their affair.

The governing element of "idha" (then) is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿So that is, that Day, a difficult day﴾ ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, for its meaning is that the matter will be hard for them. It was also said that the governing element is what is indicated by "dhalika" (that), because it is a reference to the blast. "Yawma'idhin" is a substitute for "idha," or it is a subject with the predicate ﴿a difficult day﴾, and the clause is the predicate of "dhalika." It was also said that it is an adverbial complement to the predicate, because the implied sense is: the occurrence of a difficult day.

His saying: ﴿not easy﴾ is an emphasis on its difficulty for them, because being not easy has already been understood from His saying ﴿a difficult day﴾.

﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone﴾: i.e., leave me, and this is a word of threat and warning. The meaning is: leave me with the one whom I created in the state of being alone in his mother's womb, having no wealth and no children. This is on the basis that "alone" (wahidan) is a circumstantial accusative from the relative pronoun or from the omitted returning pronoun. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial accusative from the "ya'" in "dharni," meaning: leave me alone with him, for I will suffice you in avenging yourself on him. The first is preferable.

The exegetes said: He is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

Muqatil said: He says: leave between me and him, for I will single him out for his destruction. He was singled out for mention because of the excess of his disbelief and the magnitude of his denial of Allah's blessings upon him. It was also said that by "the solitary one" is meant the one whose father is not known, and it was said about al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah that he was an adopted son (du'iya).

﴿And I made for him abundant wealth﴾: i.e., much, or that it increases in growth and increase, one thing after another.

Al-Zajjaj said: wealth not cut off from him. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah was well known for abundance of wealth in its various kinds. It was said that from the produce of his property he obtained a thousand thousand dinars, and it was said four thousand dinars, and it was said one thousand dinars.

﴿And sons present﴾: i.e., and I made for him sons present in Makkah with him, who did not travel and did not need to disperse in search of provision, because of the abundance of their father's wealth.

Al-Dahhak said: They were seven, seven born in Makkah and five born in al-Ta'if.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They were thirteen sons.

Muqatil said: They were seven, all of them men. Three of them became Muslims: Khalid, Hisham and al-Walid ibn al-Walid. After the revelation of this verse, al-Walid continued to decline in his wealth and his children until he died.

It was said that the meaning of "present" (shuhudan) is that when he is mentioned, they are mentioned with him. It was said that they used to attend what he attended and take charge of what he was engaged in.

﴿And I spread for him, spreading﴾: i.e., I extended for him in life, in long life, and in leadership among Quraysh. Tamhid (spreading) among the Arabs means preparation, and from it comes "mahd al-sabi" (the cradle of the child).

Mujahid said: It refers to property, some of it upon some, as a bed is spread.

﴿Then he desires that I should increase﴾: i.e., after all this he desires more increase, because of his great greed and intense covetousness, along with his ingratitude for blessings and his associating partners with Allah.

Al-Hasan said: Then he desires that I should admit him into Paradise. He used to say: If Muhammad is truthful, then Paradise was created only for me.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, restrained and rebuked him, saying: ﴿No!﴾, i.e., I will not increase him.

Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he has been stubborn toward Our signs﴾, i.e., opposing them and disbelieving in what We sent down from them upon Our Messenger. It is said: "anada, ya'nidu" with a kasra, when one opposes the truth and rejects it while knowing it, so he is "anid" and "ani'd." The ani'd is one who deviates from the path and turns away from the right course. From this is the words of al-Harithi:

*When I ride, make me in the middle, for I am old and cannot bear the stubborn.*

Abu Salih said: "'anid" means "distant."

Qatadah said: "jahid" (one who denies).

Muqatil said: "mu'rid" (one who turns away).

﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾: i.e., I will impose upon him a burden of punishment, and it is a parable for the difficult punishment which cannot be borne. It was also said the meaning is that he will be made to climb a mountain of fire. In the speech of the Arabs, "irhaq" means that a person carries a heavy thing.

The clause ﴿Indeed he reflected and determined﴾ gives the reason for the threat mentioned before it. That is, he reflected on the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and on the Qur'an that had been revealed to him, and he determined within himself, that is, he prepared the speech in his mind. The Arabs say "hayya'tu al-shay'" (I prepared the thing) when they mean "qaddartu," and "qaddartu al-shay'" (I determined the thing) when they mean "hayya'tu." This is because, when he heard the Qur'an, he kept reflecting on what to say about it and prepared in his mind what he would say.

So Allah censured him and said: ﴿Then he was killed, how he determined﴾. That is, he was cursed and punished for how he determined, that is, in what manner he determined what he determined of speech. This is like the saying in speech, "I will strike him however he acts," meaning in whatever manner he acts. It has also been said that the meaning is: he was overpowered and defeated, however he determined. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes shed tears only so that you may strike,*
*with your two arrows, into the parts of a pierced heart."*

Al-Zuhri said: "He was punished." This is in the form of a curse against him.

The repetition in His saying ﴿Then he was killed, how he determined﴾ is for emphasis and intensification.

﴿Then he looked﴾, that is, by what means he might repel the Qur'an and discredit it, or he reflected on the Qur'an and considered what it is.

﴿Then he frowned﴾, that is, he contracted his face because he did not find a flaw by which to attack the Qur'an. The noun "al-'abs" is the verbal noun of "'abasa" (with a light form), "ya'bisu 'absan wa 'uburran," when one frowns. It has been said that he frowned at the faces of the believers, and it has been said that he frowned at the face of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And scowled﴾, that is, his face became contorted and changed. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"We attacked Tamim at dawn of al-Hifar,*
*with a grey (horse) struck by a dark, scowling one."*

And the saying of another:

*"Her turning away has troubled me, which I saw,*
*and her aversion from my need, and her scowling."*

It has been said that the appearance of frowning on the face comes after the exchange of words, while the appearance of scowling on the face comes before it. The Arabs say "wajh basir" (a scowling face) when it has changed and turned black.

Al-Raghib said: "Al-busr" is hastening evil before its time, like "basara al-rajulu hajatahu," meaning he sought his need out of its proper time.

He said: From this is His saying ﴿frowned and scowled﴾, meaning he displayed frowning before its time and before its moment. The people of Yemen say, "basara al-markab and absara," meaning the ship stood still, neither advancing nor retreating. "Qad ubsirna" means "we have come to scowling."

﴿Then he turned his back and became arrogant﴾, that is, he turned away from the truth, went to his family, and magnified himself against believing.

﴿So he said: This is nothing but magic that is transmitted﴾, that is, he takes it from others and relates it from them.

Magic (al-sihr) is the display of falsehood in the form of truth, or deception, as its explanation was given earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. It is said "athartu al-hadith bi-atharihi" (I relayed the report by its chain) when you mention it from another. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*"What is in it, that you two contended over,*
*is clear to the listener and to the transmitted report."*

﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being﴾, meaning it is the speech of men, not the speech of Allah. This is an emphasis of what precedes it. It will come that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah only said this saying to please his people, after he had acknowledged that it has a sweetness and that it has a radiance, up to the end of his statement.

When he said this saying that Allah related about him, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿I will cast him into Saqar﴾, that is, I will make him enter the Fire. Saqar is one of the names of the Fire and one of the levels of Jahannam. It has been said that this sentence is a substitute for His saying ﴿I will force him to a steep ascent﴾.

Then He (glorified is He) exaggerated in describing the Fire and the severity of its matter, and said: ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾, that is, what will make you know what it is. The Arabs say, "wa-ma adraka ma kadha" (and what will make you know what such-and-such is) when they want to exaggerate its matter, magnify its affair and make its calamity terrifying. The first "ma" is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿what Saqar is﴾ is its predicate.

Then He explained its state, saying: ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾. The clause is resumptive, to explain the state of Saqar and to reveal its description. It has been said that it is in a place of accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element in it is the meaning of magnification, because His saying ﴿and what will make you know what Saqar is﴾ indicates magnification, as if He said: "Magnify Saqar in this state." The first view is better. The object of the two verbs is omitted.

Al-Suddi said: "It leaves for them no flesh and leaves for them no bone."

Ata' said: "It leaves none within it alive, nor leaves it dead." It has also been said that they are two words with one meaning, repeated for emphasis, like your saying "sadda 'anni" and "a'rada 'anni" (he turned away from me and he avoided me).

﴿Scorching to the human being﴾. The majority read ﴿Scorching﴾ with a nominative ending, as the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'). It has been said that it is an adjective of Saqar, and the first is better.

Al-Hasan, 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi, Nasr ibn 'Asim, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with an accusative ending, as a circumstantial clause (hal) or as a specification for the sake of terror. It is said: "laha yaluhu," meaning it appeared; the meaning is that it appears to the human beings.

Al-Hasan said: "Jahannam shows itself to them until they see it directly," like His saying: ﴿And Hell is brought forth for whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿scorching to the human being﴾ is that it changes them and blackens them.

Mujahid said: "The Arabs say: 'laha al-harr wa-l-bard wa-l-saqam wa-l-huzn' (the heat, the cold, the sickness, and the sorrow scorched him) when it changed him." This is more preponderant than the first view, and most of the exegetes adopted it. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Hind wonders when she saw me emaciated,*
*she says: 'What thing has been scorched by the poisonous winds?'"*

That is, it changed him. From this is the saying of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

*"It scorched him after robustness and youth,*
*like your scorching of a lean camel folded for the race."*

Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is that it makes the human beings thirsty. He recited:

*"It gave me to drink, on a plate of water, a draught,*
*which God gave it to drink with the abundant rains."*

By "human beings" (al-bashar) is meant either the outer skin of a person, as most have said, or the meaning is the people of the Fire from mankind, as al-Akhfash said.

﴿Over it are nineteen﴾. The exegetes said: That is, over the Fire are nineteen of the angels, who are its guardians. It has been said: nineteen categories of the types of angels. It has been said: nineteen rows of their rows. It has been said: nineteen chiefs, with each chief a company of angels. The first is better.

Al-Tha'labi said: "This is not to be denied; if one angel takes the souls of all creatures, it is more fitting that they be nineteen over the punishment of some of creation."

The majority read ﴿nineteen﴾ with the shin of ('ashara) vocalized with a fatha. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Talhah ibn Sulayman read it with a sukun.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman said: "The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾." Yahya ibn Abi Kathir said to him: (p-1553) "They say the first to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [i.e., Surat al-'Alaq]." Abu Salamah said: "I asked Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah about that, I said to him the same as I said, and Jabir said: 'I will not relate to you except what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to us: "I secluded myself in Hira'. When I completed my seclusion, I descended, and I was called. I looked to my right and saw nothing, I looked to my left and saw nothing, I looked behind me and saw nothing. I raised my head and saw the angel who had come to me at Hira' sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth. I was seized with terror from him, so I returned and said: 'Wrap me up, wrap me up!' So they wrapped me up, and there was revealed ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, ﴿Arise and warn﴾ up to His saying ﴿and abandon the idols﴾."' It will come in Surat 'Iqra' what indicates that it is the first surah revealed, and the combination is possible.

Al-Hakim related and authenticated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ that he said: "Wrap up this matter and rise with it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from him concerning ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ that he said: "The sleeper." ﴿And your garments, purify﴾: "Let not your garments that you wear be from an unlawful earning." ﴿And the idol, abandon﴾: "The idols." ﴿And do not confer favor seeking more﴾: "Do not give seeking to get more than it in return."

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from him also concerning ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ that he said: "From sin." He said: "And it is in the speech of the Arabs: clean garments."

Ibn Mardawayh related from him also concerning ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ that he said: "From treachery; do not be a treacherous one."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Ikrimah, from him also, that he was asked about His saying ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ and he said: "Do not wear them over treachery." Then he said: "Do you not hear the saying of Ghaylan ibn Salamah:

*"And by the praise of Allah, I have not worn the garment of a wicked one,*
*nor do I cover myself with a garment of treachery."*

Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from him also concerning ﴿And do not confer favor seeking more﴾ that he said: "Do not give a man a gift hoping that he will give you more than it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from him also concerning ﴿So when the trumpet is sounded﴾ that he said: "The Horn." ﴿It will be a difficult day﴾: "Severe."

Ibn Mardawayh related from him also concerning ﴿Leave me with whom I created alone﴾ that he said: "Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah."

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from him also: "That al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he recited the Qur'an to him, so it seemed he softened to it. This reached Abu Jahl, so he came to him and said: 'O uncle, your people want to gather wealth for you to give to you, for you came to Muhammad to oppose what he received.' He said: 'Quraysh know that I am among the most wealthy of them.' He said: 'Then say about him a saying by which your people will learn that you deny it and that you hate it.' He said: 'And what should I say? By Allah, there is not among you a man more knowledgeable of poetry than I, neither of its rajaz nor its qasida, nor of the poetry of the jinn. By Allah, what he says does not resemble any of this at all. By Allah, his saying has a sweetness, and it has a radiance, and it is fruitful at its top and abundant at its base, and it rises and nothing rises above it, and it breaks what is beneath it.' He said: 'By Allah, your people will not be pleased until you say something about him.' He said: 'Leave me until I reflect.' When he reflected he said: 'This is magic that is transmitted; he takes it from others.' So there was revealed ﴿Leave me with whom I created alone﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq related this from 'Ikrimah as a mursal (a report with a missing companion in the chain), and likewise Ibn Jarir, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he was asked about His saying ﴿And I made for him abundant wealth﴾ and he said: "The produce of one month after another month."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿And I made for him abundant wealth﴾ that he said: "A thousand dinars."

Hannad related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning His saying ﴿I will force him to a steep ascent﴾ that he said: "It is a mountain in the Fire; they are commanded to climb it, and whenever they place their hands upon it, it melts, and when they lift them, it returns as it was."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿stubborn﴾ that he said: "Denying."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The steep ascent (al-su'ud) is a mountain in the Fire; the disbeliever climbs it for seventy autumns, then he falls down, and he remains like that in it forever."

Al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: "It is strange; we do not know it except from the hadith of Ibn Lahi'ah from Darraj."

Ibn Kathir said: "In it there is strangeness and irregularity." End of quote. It was related by a group of people as the saying of Abu Sa'id. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "'Su'ud' is a rock in Jahannam over which the disbeliever is dragged on his face."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him: "A mountain in the Fire."

Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning His saying ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾ that he said: "It leaves none of them anything. And when they are given another creation, it does not leave them to return to the first punishment."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from him also ﴿Scorching to the human being﴾: "It scorches the skin and burns it and changes its color, so it becomes blacker than the night."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also ﴿Scorching﴾: "Burning."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from al-Bara': that a group of Jews asked some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the guardians of Jahannam. He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." Then Jibril came and informed the Prophet (ﷺ), and at that moment there was revealed to him ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾.

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: Surat al-Muddaththir was revealed in Makkah.

Ibn Mardawayh related the same from Ibn al-Zubayr, and it will come that the beginning of this surah was the first part of the Qur'an to be revealed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes (mufassirun) said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was first visited by revelation, Jibril came to him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him upon a throne between the heaven and the earth, like a dazzling light. He was terrified and fell unconscious. When he recovered, he entered upon Khadijah and asked for water, which she poured over him, and he said: "Wrap me up, wrap me up!" So they wrapped him in a cloak, and then (Allah) said: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ ﴿Arise and warn﴾.

The meaning of ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ is: O you who have wrapped himself in his garments, i.e., covered himself with them. Its origin is al-mutadaththir, and the letter ta was assimilated into the dal because they are similar in articulation (idgham, assimilation).

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) recited it with assimilation, while Ubayy read al-mutadaththir according to the original form. Al-dithar is what is worn over al-shi'ar, and al-shi'ar is what lies next to the body. Ikrimah said: the meaning is, O you who are wrapped up in prophethood and its burdens.

Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a far-fetched metaphor, because he was not yet a prophet at that time.

﴿Arise and warn﴾: i.e., stand up, and frighten the people of Makkah and warn them of the punishment if they do not submit (to Islam). Or: rise from your bed. Or: rise with resolve and determination. It was also said that warning here means informing them of his prophethood, and it was said it means informing them of tawhid (the Oneness of Allah).

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: stand and pray, and command the prayer.

﴿And your Lord, glorify﴾: i.e., single out your Master, your Owner and the one who sets your affairs right, with magnification (takbir). It means describing Him, glory be to Him, with greatness and majesty, that He is far greater than having any partner, as the disbelievers believe, and far greater than having a consort or a son.

Ibn al-Arabi said: What is meant is the takbir of sanctification and transcendence, by stripping away opposites, rivals and idols, not taking any protector other than Him, not worshipping anyone besides Him, not seeing any act as belonging to anyone other than Him, and no blessing except from Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: The fa' in ﴿so glorify﴾ entered with the sense of a condition (jaza'), as it entered in ﴿so warn﴾.

Ibn Jinni said: It is like your saying: "Zaydan, so strike" meaning "Zayd, strike," so the fa' is superfluous.

﴿And your garments, purify﴾: What is meant by them is the garments that are worn, according to the linguistic meaning. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to purify his garments and keep them safe from impurities (najasat), and to remove whatever impurity had fallen on them. It was also said that what is meant by "garments" is deeds, or the heart, or the soul, or the body, or the family, or the religion, or the character.

Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Abu Razin said: i.e., your deeds, so set them right.

Qatadah said: Purify your soul from sin, and "garments" is an expression for the soul.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: purify your heart. From this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*So bid farewell to my garments, from your garments you shall be stripped*

Ikrimah said: The meaning is: wear them without treachery and without immorality.

He also said: Have you not heard the words of the poet:

*And by the praise of Allah, I have worn no garment of an immoral man, nor do I cover myself with treachery.*

The poet is Ghaylan ibn Salamah al-Thaqafi. An example of using "garments" for the self is the words of Antarah:

*So I pierced with the long spear his garments; the noble man is not forbidden on the spear-point.*

And the words of another:

*The garments of the Banu Awf are pure and clean.*

Al-Hasan and al-Qurazi said: The meaning is: purify your character (akhlaq), because a person's character encompasses his states just as his garments encompass his body. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Yahya is not blamed for bad character, and Yahya is pure of garment, free.*

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: ﴿and your garments, shorten﴾, because shortening the garment keeps it further from impurities when it trails on the ground. Tawus also said this, but the first (view) is preferable because it is the literal meaning.

There is no figurative use of "garments" for something else by way of a relation with a clear indicator that shows it is intended when used absolutely, and there is no disagreement on such a principle, namely taking the literal meaning when a word is used without qualification. In this verse there is evidence for the obligation of purity of garments in the prayer.

﴿And the abomination, abandon﴾: al-rujz in the language means punishment, and it has two readings: with a kasra on the ra' and with a damma. Polytheism and the worship of idols were called rujz because they are the cause of punishment.

The majority read al-rujz with a kasra on the ra'.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Hafs and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a damma.

Mujahid and Ikrimah said: al-rujz is the idols, as in His saying: ﴿So avoid the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. Ibn Zayd also said this.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: al-rijz is sin, and al-hajr means abandonment.

Qatadah said: al-rijz is Isaf and Na'ilah, two idols that were beside the House.

Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi' and al-Kisai said: al-rujz with a damma is the idol, and with a kasra is the punishment.

Al-Suddi said: al-rijz with a damma on the ra' is the threat. The first (view) is preferable.

﴿And do not bestow favour seeking to gain more﴾: The majority read ﴿do not bestow favour﴾ (la tamnun) with the separation of the doubled letters (fakk al-idgham), while al-Hasan, Abu al-Yaman and al-Ashhab al-Uqayli read it with idgham. The majority read ﴿seeking to gain more﴾ (tasta'kthiru) with a damma, on the basis that it is a circumstantial clause (hal): i.e., do not bestow favour while being one who seeks to gain more. It was also said that it is on the basis of the omission of "an" (that), the original being: do not bestow favour that you seek to gain more, and when "an" was omitted, it became marfu'.

Al-Kisai said: When "an" is omitted, the verb takes the damma.

Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read tastakthir with the addition of "an."

Al-Hasan also, and Ibn Abi Ablah, read tastakthir with a jazm (apocopated form), on the basis that it is a substitute (badal) for tamnun, as in His saying: ﴿he will meet a penalty﴾ ﴿it will be multiplied for him﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], and the words of the poet:

*If you come to us, you will visit us at our homes, and find firewood, thick and a blazing fire.*

Or the jazm is because the connected form is treated as the pause form, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*So today I drink, not bearing a sin from Allah, nor a bold intruder.*

with the sukun on "ashrab."

This reading has been objected to, because "tastakthiru" cannot be a substitute for "tamnun," since bestowing favour is other than seeking to gain more, and it cannot be a response to the prohibition (jawab al-nahy).

The predecessors (al-salaf) differed about the meaning of the verse. It was said: The meaning is: do not bestow favour upon your Lord for the burdens of prophethood that you bear, like one who considers what he bears on account of others to be great. It was said: Do not give a gift seeking in it something better than it, as said by Ikrimah and Qatadah.

Al-Dahhak said: This was forbidden by Allah to His Messenger, because he was commanded with the noblest manners and the most sublime character, and He permitted it to his community.

Mujahid said: Do not weaken in seeking to gain more of good, from your saying "a strong rope" when it is weak.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Do not make your deed great in your own eyes by seeking to gain more of good.

Ibn Kaysan said: Do not consider a deed great so that you see it as coming from yourself; rather, your deed is a favour from Allah upon you, since He made a way for you to His worship.

It was also said: Do not bestow favour through prophethood and the Qur'an upon the people, so that you take from them a wage that you consider great.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Do not give your wealth as a means of flattery.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: When you give a gift, give it for your Lord.

﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾: i.e., for the sake of the face of your Lord, be patient in obeying Him and in His obligations. The meaning is: for the sake of your Lord and His reward.

Muqatil and Mujahid said: be patient over harm and denial.

Ibn Zayd said: You have borne a great matter, and the Arabs and non-Arabs will fight you, so be patient over it for Allah's sake.

It was said: be patient under the decrees of destiny for Allah's sake. It was said: be patient over trials. It was said: be patient over the commands and prohibitions.

﴿So when the trumpet is blown﴾: al-naqur is on the pattern fa'ul from al-naqr, as if it is something into which one blows to make a sound. In the speech of the Arabs, al-naqr means sound, and from it is the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*I lower it with a sound when I have raised it.*

They say: "naqara bi-ism al-rajul" when he called the man by name. What is meant here is the blowing into the Trumpet (al-Sur), and what is meant is the second blast, though it was also said the first. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat al-An'am and Surat al-Nahl. The fa' is for causation, as if it were said: be patient over their harm, for before them is a terrifying day in which they will meet the outcome of their affair.

The governing element of "idha" (then) is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿So that is, that Day, a difficult day﴾ ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, for its meaning is that the matter will be hard for them. It was also said that the governing element is what is indicated by "dhalika" (that), because it is a reference to the blast. "Yawma'idhin" is a substitute for "idha," or it is a subject with the predicate ﴿a difficult day﴾, and the clause is the predicate of "dhalika." It was also said that it is an adverbial complement to the predicate, because the implied sense is: the occurrence of a difficult day.

His saying: ﴿not easy﴾ is an emphasis on its difficulty for them, because being not easy has already been understood from His saying ﴿a difficult day﴾.

﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone﴾: i.e., leave me, and this is a word of threat and warning. The meaning is: leave me with the one whom I created in the state of being alone in his mother's womb, having no wealth and no children. This is on the basis that "alone" (wahidan) is a circumstantial accusative from the relative pronoun or from the omitted returning pronoun. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial accusative from the "ya'" in "dharni," meaning: leave me alone with him, for I will suffice you in avenging yourself on him. The first is preferable.

The exegetes said: He is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

Muqatil said: He says: leave between me and him, for I will single him out for his destruction. He was singled out for mention because of the excess of his disbelief and the magnitude of his denial of Allah's blessings upon him. It was also said that by "the solitary one" is meant the one whose father is not known, and it was said about al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah that he was an adopted son (du'iya).

﴿And I made for him abundant wealth﴾: i.e., much, or that it increases in growth and increase, one thing after another.

Al-Zajjaj said: wealth not cut off from him. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah was well known for abundance of wealth in its various kinds. It was said that from the produce of his property he obtained a thousand thousand dinars, and it was said four thousand dinars, and it was said one thousand dinars.

﴿And sons present﴾: i.e., and I made for him sons present in Makkah with him, who did not travel and did not need to disperse in search of provision, because of the abundance of their father's wealth.

Al-Dahhak said: They were seven, seven born in Makkah and five born in al-Ta'if.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They were thirteen sons.

Muqatil said: They were seven, all of them men. Three of them became Muslims: Khalid, Hisham and al-Walid ibn al-Walid. After the revelation of this verse, al-Walid continued to decline in his wealth and his children until he died.

It was said that the meaning of "present" (shuhudan) is that when he is mentioned, they are mentioned with him. It was said that they used to attend what he attended and take charge of what he was engaged in.

﴿And I spread for him, spreading﴾: i.e., I extended for him in life, in long life, and in leadership among Quraysh. Tamhid (spreading) among the Arabs means preparation, and from it comes "mahd al-sabi" (the cradle of the child).

Mujahid said: It refers to property, some of it upon some, as a bed is spread.

﴿Then he desires that I should increase﴾: i.e., after all this he desires more increase, because of his great greed and intense covetousness, along with his ingratitude for blessings and his associating partners with Allah.

Al-Hasan said: Then he desires that I should admit him into Paradise. He used to say: If Muhammad is truthful, then Paradise was created only for me.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, restrained and rebuked him, saying: ﴿No!﴾, i.e., I will not increase him.

Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he has been stubborn toward Our signs﴾, i.e., opposing them and disbelieving in what We sent down from them upon Our Messenger. It is said: "anada, ya'nidu" with a kasra, when one opposes the truth and rejects it while knowing it, so he is "anid" and "ani'd." The ani'd is one who deviates from the path and turns away from the right course. From this is the words of al-Harithi:

*When I ride, make me in the middle, for I am old and cannot bear the stubborn.*

Abu Salih said: "'anid" means "distant."

Qatadah said: "jahid" (one who denies).

Muqatil said: "mu'rid" (one who turns away).

﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾: i.e., I will impose upon him a burden of punishment, and it is a parable for the difficult punishment which cannot be borne. It was also said the meaning is that he will be made to climb a mountain of fire. In the speech of the Arabs, "irhaq" means that a person carries a heavy thing.

The clause ﴿Indeed he reflected and determined﴾ gives the reason for the threat mentioned before it. That is, he reflected on the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and on the Qur'an that had been revealed to him, and he determined within himself, that is, he prepared the speech in his mind. The Arabs say "hayya'tu al-shay'" (I prepared the thing) when they mean "qaddartu," and "qaddartu al-shay'" (I determined the thing) when they mean "hayya'tu." This is because, when he heard the Qur'an, he kept reflecting on what to say about it and prepared in his mind what he would say.

So Allah censured him and said: ﴿Then he was killed, how he determined﴾. That is, he was cursed and punished for how he determined, that is, in what manner he determined what he determined of speech. This is like the saying in speech, "I will strike him however he acts," meaning in whatever manner he acts. It has also been said that the meaning is: he was overpowered and defeated, however he determined. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes shed tears only so that you may strike,*
*with your two arrows, into the parts of a pierced heart."*

Al-Zuhri said: "He was punished." This is in the form of a curse against him.

The repetition in His saying ﴿Then he was killed, how he determined﴾ is for emphasis and intensification.

﴿Then he looked﴾, that is, by what means he might repel the Qur'an and discredit it, or he reflected on the Qur'an and considered what it is.

﴿Then he frowned﴾, that is, he contracted his face because he did not find a flaw by which to attack the Qur'an. The noun "al-'abs" is the verbal noun of "'abasa" (with a light form), "ya'bisu 'absan wa 'uburran," when one frowns. It has been said that he frowned at the faces of the believers, and it has been said that he frowned at the face of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And scowled﴾, that is, his face became contorted and changed. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"We attacked Tamim at dawn of al-Hifar,*
*with a grey (horse) struck by a dark, scowling one."*

And the saying of another:

*"Her turning away has troubled me, which I saw,*
*and her aversion from my need, and her scowling."*

It has been said that the appearance of frowning on the face comes after the exchange of words, while the appearance of scowling on the face comes before it. The Arabs say "wajh basir" (a scowling face) when it has changed and turned black.

Al-Raghib said: "Al-busr" is hastening evil before its time, like "basara al-rajulu hajatahu," meaning he sought his need out of its proper time.

He said: From this is His saying ﴿frowned and scowled﴾, meaning he displayed frowning before its time and before its moment. The people of Yemen say, "basara al-markab and absara," meaning the ship stood still, neither advancing nor retreating. "Qad ubsirna" means "we have come to scowling."

﴿Then he turned his back and became arrogant﴾, that is, he turned away from the truth, went to his family, and magnified himself against believing.

﴿So he said: This is nothing but magic that is transmitted﴾, that is, he takes it from others and relates it from them.

Magic (al-sihr) is the display of falsehood in the form of truth, or deception, as its explanation was given earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. It is said "athartu al-hadith bi-atharihi" (I relayed the report by its chain) when you mention it from another. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*"What is in it, that you two contended over,*
*is clear to the listener and to the transmitted report."*

﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being﴾, meaning it is the speech of men, not the speech of Allah. This is an emphasis of what precedes it. It will come that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah only said this saying to please his people, after he had acknowledged that it has a sweetness and that it has a radiance, up to the end of his statement.

When he said this saying that Allah related about him, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿I will cast him into Saqar﴾, that is, I will make him enter the Fire. Saqar is one of the names of the Fire and one of the levels of Jahannam. It has been said that this sentence is a substitute for His saying ﴿I will force him to a steep ascent﴾.

Then He (glorified is He) exaggerated in describing the Fire and the severity of its matter, and said: ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾, that is, what will make you know what it is. The Arabs say, "wa-ma adraka ma kadha" (and what will make you know what such-and-such is) when they want to exaggerate its matter, magnify its affair and make its calamity terrifying. The first "ma" is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿what Saqar is﴾ is its predicate.

Then He explained its state, saying: ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾. The clause is resumptive, to explain the state of Saqar and to reveal its description. It has been said that it is in a place of accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element in it is the meaning of magnification, because His saying ﴿and what will make you know what Saqar is﴾ indicates magnification, as if He said: "Magnify Saqar in this state." The first view is better. The object of the two verbs is omitted.

Al-Suddi said: "It leaves for them no flesh and leaves for them no bone."

Ata' said: "It leaves none within it alive, nor leaves it dead." It has also been said that they are two words with one meaning, repeated for emphasis, like your saying "sadda 'anni" and "a'rada 'anni" (he turned away from me and he avoided me).

﴿Scorching to the human being﴾. The majority read ﴿Scorching﴾ with a nominative ending, as the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'). It has been said that it is an adjective of Saqar, and the first is better.

Al-Hasan, 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi, Nasr ibn 'Asim, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with an accusative ending, as a circumstantial clause (hal) or as a specification for the sake of terror. It is said: "laha yaluhu," meaning it appeared; the meaning is that it appears to the human beings.

Al-Hasan said: "Jahannam shows itself to them until they see it directly," like His saying: ﴿And Hell is brought forth for whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿scorching to the human being﴾ is that it changes them and blackens them.

Mujahid said: "The Arabs say: 'laha al-harr wa-l-bard wa-l-saqam wa-l-huzn' (the heat, the cold, the sickness, and the sorrow scorched him) when it changed him." This is more preponderant than the first view, and most of the exegetes adopted it. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"Hind wonders when she saw me emaciated,*
*she says: 'What thing has been scorched by the poisonous winds?'"*

That is, it changed him. From this is the saying of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

*"It scorched him after robustness and youth,*
*like your scorching of a lean camel folded for the race."*

Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is that it makes the human beings thirsty. He recited:

*"It gave me to drink, on a plate of water, a draught,*
*which God gave it to drink with the abundant rains."*

By "human beings" (al-bashar) is meant either the outer skin of a person, as most have said, or the meaning is the people of the Fire from mankind, as al-Akhfash said.

﴿Over it are nineteen﴾. The exegetes said: That is, over the Fire are nineteen of the angels, who are its guardians. It has been said: nineteen categories of the types of angels. It has been said: nineteen rows of their rows. It has been said: nineteen chiefs, with each chief a company of angels. The first is better.

Al-Tha'labi said: "This is not to be denied; if one angel takes the souls of all creatures, it is more fitting that they be nineteen over the punishment of some of creation."

The majority read ﴿nineteen﴾ with the shin of ('ashara) vocalized with a fatha. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Talhah ibn Sulayman read it with a sukun.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman said: "The first of the Qur'an to be revealed was ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾." Yahya ibn Abi Kathir said to him: (p-1553) "They say the first to be revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [i.e., Surat al-'Alaq]." Abu Salamah said: "I asked Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah about that, I said to him the same as I said, and Jabir said: 'I will not relate to you except what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related to us: "I secluded myself in Hira'. When I completed my seclusion, I descended, and I was called. I looked to my right and saw nothing, I looked to my left and saw nothing, I looked behind me and saw nothing. I raised my head and saw the angel who had come to me at Hira' sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth. I was seized with terror from him, so I returned and said: 'Wrap me up, wrap me up!' So they wrapped me up, and there was revealed ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, ﴿Arise and warn﴾ up to His saying ﴿and abandon the idols﴾."' It will come in Surat 'Iqra' what indicates that it is the first surah revealed, and the combination is possible.

Al-Hakim related and authenticated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ that he said: "Wrap up this matter and rise with it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from him concerning ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ that he said: "The sleeper." ﴿And your garments, purify﴾: "Let not your garments that you wear be from an unlawful earning." ﴿And the idol, abandon﴾: "The idols." ﴿And do not confer favor seeking more﴾: "Do not give seeking to get more than it in return."

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from him also concerning ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ that he said: "From sin." He said: "And it is in the speech of the Arabs: clean garments."

Ibn Mardawayh related from him also concerning ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ that he said: "From treachery; do not be a treacherous one."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Ikrimah, from him also, that he was asked about His saying ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ and he said: "Do not wear them over treachery." Then he said: "Do you not hear the saying of Ghaylan ibn Salamah:

*"And by the praise of Allah, I have not worn the garment of a wicked one,*
*nor do I cover myself with a garment of treachery."*

Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from him also concerning ﴿And do not confer favor seeking more﴾ that he said: "Do not give a man a gift hoping that he will give you more than it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from him also concerning ﴿So when the trumpet is sounded﴾ that he said: "The Horn." ﴿It will be a difficult day﴾: "Severe."

Ibn Mardawayh related from him also concerning ﴿Leave me with whom I created alone﴾ that he said: "Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah."

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from him also: "That al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he recited the Qur'an to him, so it seemed he softened to it. This reached Abu Jahl, so he came to him and said: 'O uncle, your people want to gather wealth for you to give to you, for you came to Muhammad to oppose what he received.' He said: 'Quraysh know that I am among the most wealthy of them.' He said: 'Then say about him a saying by which your people will learn that you deny it and that you hate it.' He said: 'And what should I say? By Allah, there is not among you a man more knowledgeable of poetry than I, neither of its rajaz nor its qasida, nor of the poetry of the jinn. By Allah, what he says does not resemble any of this at all. By Allah, his saying has a sweetness, and it has a radiance, and it is fruitful at its top and abundant at its base, and it rises and nothing rises above it, and it breaks what is beneath it.' He said: 'By Allah, your people will not be pleased until you say something about him.' He said: 'Leave me until I reflect.' When he reflected he said: 'This is magic that is transmitted; he takes it from others.' So there was revealed ﴿Leave me with whom I created alone﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq related this from 'Ikrimah as a mursal (a report with a missing companion in the chain), and likewise Ibn Jarir, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he was asked about His saying ﴿And I made for him abundant wealth﴾ and he said: "The produce of one month after another month."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿And I made for him abundant wealth﴾ that he said: "A thousand dinars."

Hannad related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning His saying ﴿I will force him to a steep ascent﴾ that he said: "It is a mountain in the Fire; they are commanded to climb it, and whenever they place their hands upon it, it melts, and when they lift them, it returns as it was."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿stubborn﴾ that he said: "Denying."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The steep ascent (al-su'ud) is a mountain in the Fire; the disbeliever climbs it for seventy autumns, then he falls down, and he remains like that in it forever."

Al-Tirmidhi said after relating it: "It is strange; we do not know it except from the hadith of Ibn Lahi'ah from Darraj."

Ibn Kathir said: "In it there is strangeness and irregularity." End of quote. It was related by a group of people as the saying of Abu Sa'id. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "'Su'ud' is a rock in Jahannam over which the disbeliever is dragged on his face."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him: "A mountain in the Fire."

Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning His saying ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾ that he said: "It leaves none of them anything. And when they are given another creation, it does not leave them to return to the first punishment."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from him also ﴿Scorching to the human being﴾: "It scorches the skin and burns it and changes its color, so it becomes blacker than the night."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also ﴿Scorching﴾: "Burning."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th related from al-Bara': that a group of Jews asked some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) about the guardians of Jahannam. He said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." Then Jibril came and informed the Prophet (ﷺ), and at that moment there was revealed to him ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾.

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: Surat al-Muddaththir was revealed in Makkah.

Ibn Mardawayh related the same from Ibn al-Zubayr, and it will come that the beginning of this surah was the first part of the Qur'an to be revealed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes (mufassirun) said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was first visited by revelation, Jibril came to him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him upon a throne between the heaven and the earth, like a dazzling light. He was terrified and fell unconscious. When he recovered, he entered upon Khadijah and asked for water, which she poured over him, and he said: "Wrap me up, wrap me up!" So they wrapped him in a cloak, and then (Allah) said: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ ﴿Arise and warn﴾.

The meaning of ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ is: O you who have wrapped himself in his garments, i.e., covered himself with them. Its origin is al-mutadaththir, and the letter ta was assimilated into the dal because they are similar in articulation (idgham, assimilation).

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) recited it with assimilation, while Ubayy read al-mutadaththir according to the original form. Al-dithar is what is worn over al-shi'ar, and al-shi'ar is what lies next to the body. Ikrimah said: the meaning is, O you who are wrapped up in prophethood and its burdens.

Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a far-fetched metaphor, because he was not yet a prophet at that time.

﴿Arise and warn﴾: i.e., stand up, and frighten the people of Makkah and warn them of the punishment if they do not submit (to Islam). Or: rise from your bed. Or: rise with resolve and determination. It was also said that warning here means informing them of his prophethood, and it was said it means informing them of tawhid (the Oneness of Allah).

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: stand and pray, and command the prayer.

﴿And your Lord, glorify﴾: i.e., single out your Master, your Owner and the one who sets your affairs right, with magnification (takbir). It means describing Him, glory be to Him, with greatness and majesty, that He is far greater than having any partner, as the disbelievers believe, and far greater than having a consort or a son.

Ibn al-Arabi said: What is meant is the takbir of sanctification and transcendence, by stripping away opposites, rivals and idols, not taking any protector other than Him, not worshipping anyone besides Him, not seeing any act as belonging to anyone other than Him, and no blessing except from Him.

Al-Zajjaj said: The fa' in ﴿so glorify﴾ entered with the sense of a condition (jaza'), as it entered in ﴿so warn﴾.

Ibn Jinni said: It is like your saying: "Zaydan, so strike" meaning "Zayd, strike," so the fa' is superfluous.

﴿And your garments, purify﴾: What is meant by them is the garments that are worn, according to the linguistic meaning. Allah, glory be to Him, commanded him to purify his garments and keep them safe from impurities (najasat), and to remove whatever impurity had fallen on them. It was also said that what is meant by "garments" is deeds, or the heart, or the soul, or the body, or the family, or the religion, or the character.

Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Abu Razin said: i.e., your deeds, so set them right.

Qatadah said: Purify your soul from sin, and "garments" is an expression for the soul.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: purify your heart. From this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*So bid farewell to my garments, from your garments you shall be stripped*

Ikrimah said: The meaning is: wear them without treachery and without immorality.

He also said: Have you not heard the words of the poet:

*And by the praise of Allah, I have worn no garment of an immoral man, nor do I cover myself with treachery.*

The poet is Ghaylan ibn Salamah al-Thaqafi. An example of using "garments" for the self is the words of Antarah:

*So I pierced with the long spear his garments; the noble man is not forbidden on the spear-point.*

And the words of another:

*The garments of the Banu Awf are pure and clean.*

Al-Hasan and al-Qurazi said: The meaning is: purify your character (akhlaq), because a person's character encompasses his states just as his garments encompass his body. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Yahya is not blamed for bad character, and Yahya is pure of garment, free.*

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: ﴿and your garments, shorten﴾, because shortening the garment keeps it further from impurities when it trails on the ground. Tawus also said this, but the first (view) is preferable because it is the literal meaning.

There is no figurative use of "garments" for something else by way of a relation with a clear indicator that shows it is intended when used absolutely, and there is no disagreement on such a principle, namely taking the literal meaning when a word is used without qualification. In this verse there is evidence for the obligation of purity of garments in the prayer.

﴿And the abomination, abandon﴾: al-rujz in the language means punishment, and it has two readings: with a kasra on the ra' and with a damma. Polytheism and the worship of idols were called rujz because they are the cause of punishment.

The majority read al-rujz with a kasra on the ra'.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ikrimah, Hafs and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a damma.

Mujahid and Ikrimah said: al-rujz is the idols, as in His saying: ﴿So avoid the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. Ibn Zayd also said this.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: al-rijz is sin, and al-hajr means abandonment.

Qatadah said: al-rijz is Isaf and Na'ilah, two idols that were beside the House.

Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi' and al-Kisai said: al-rujz with a damma is the idol, and with a kasra is the punishment.

Al-Suddi said: al-rijz with a damma on the ra' is the threat. The first (view) is preferable.

﴿And do not bestow favour seeking to gain more﴾: The majority read ﴿do not bestow favour﴾ (la tamnun) with the separation of the doubled letters (fakk al-idgham), while al-Hasan, Abu al-Yaman and al-Ashhab al-Uqayli read it with idgham. The majority read ﴿seeking to gain more﴾ (tasta'kthiru) with a damma, on the basis that it is a circumstantial clause (hal): i.e., do not bestow favour while being one who seeks to gain more. It was also said that it is on the basis of the omission of "an" (that), the original being: do not bestow favour that you seek to gain more, and when "an" was omitted, it became marfu'.

Al-Kisai said: When "an" is omitted, the verb takes the damma.

Yahya ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read tastakthir with the addition of "an."

Al-Hasan also, and Ibn Abi Ablah, read tastakthir with a jazm (apocopated form), on the basis that it is a substitute (badal) for tamnun, as in His saying: ﴿he will meet a penalty﴾ ﴿it will be multiplied for him﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], and the words of the poet:

*If you come to us, you will visit us at our homes, and find firewood, thick and a blazing fire.*

Or the jazm is because the connected form is treated as the pause form, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*So today I drink, not bearing a sin from Allah, nor a bold intruder.*

with the sukun on "ashrab."

This reading has been objected to, because "tastakthiru" cannot be a substitute for "tamnun," since bestowing favour is other than seeking to gain more, and it cannot be a response to the prohibition (jawab al-nahy).

The predecessors (al-salaf) differed about the meaning of the verse. It was said: The meaning is: do not bestow favour upon your Lord for the burdens of prophethood that you bear, like one who considers what he bears on account of others to be great. It was said: Do not give a gift seeking in it something better than it, as said by Ikrimah and Qatadah.

Al-Dahhak said: This was forbidden by Allah to His Messenger, because he was commanded with the noblest manners and the most sublime character, and He permitted it to his community.

Mujahid said: Do not weaken in seeking to gain more of good, from your saying "a strong rope" when it is weak.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Do not make your deed great in your own eyes by seeking to gain more of good.

Ibn Kaysan said: Do not consider a deed great so that you see it as coming from yourself; rather, your deed is a favour from Allah upon you, since He made a way for you to His worship.

It was also said: Do not bestow favour through prophethood and the Qur'an upon the people, so that you take from them a wage that you consider great.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Do not give your wealth as a means of flattery.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: When you give a gift, give it for your Lord.

﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾: i.e., for the sake of the face of your Lord, be patient in obeying Him and in His obligations. The meaning is: for the sake of your Lord and His reward.

Muqatil and Mujahid said: be patient over harm and denial.

Ibn Zayd said: You have borne a great matter, and the Arabs and non-Arabs will fight you, so be patient over it for Allah's sake.

It was said: be patient under the decrees of destiny for Allah's sake. It was said: be patient over trials. It was said: be patient over the commands and prohibitions.

﴿So when the trumpet is blown﴾: al-naqur is on the pattern fa'ul from al-naqr, as if it is something into which one blows to make a sound. In the speech of the Arabs, al-naqr means sound, and from it is the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*I lower it with a sound when I have raised it.*

They say: "naqara bi-ism al-rajul" when he called the man by name. What is meant here is the blowing into the Trumpet (al-Sur), and what is meant is the second blast, though it was also said the first. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat al-An'am and Surat al-Nahl. The fa' is for causation, as if it were said: be patient over their harm, for before them is a terrifying day in which they will meet the outcome of their affair.

The governing element of "idha" (then) is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿So that is, that Day, a difficult day﴾ ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, for its meaning is that the matter will be hard for them. It was also said that the governing element is what is indicated by "dhalika" (that), because it is a reference to the blast. "Yawma'idhin" is a substitute for "idha," or it is a subject with the predicate ﴿a difficult day﴾, and the clause is the predicate of "dhalika." It was also said that it is an adverbial complement to the predicate, because the implied sense is: the occurrence of a difficult day.

His saying: ﴿not easy﴾ is an emphasis on its difficulty for them, because being not easy has already been understood from His saying ﴿a difficult day﴾.

﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone﴾: i.e., leave me, and this is a word of threat and warning. The meaning is: leave me with the one whom I created in the state of being alone in his mother's womb, having no wealth and no children. This is on the basis that "alone" (wahidan) is a circumstantial accusative from the relative pronoun or from the omitted returning pronoun. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial accusative from the "ya'" in "dharni," meaning: leave me alone with him, for I will suffice you in avenging yourself on him. The first is preferable.

The exegetes said: He is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

Muqatil said: He says: leave between me and him, for I will single him out for his destruction. He was singled out for mention because of the excess of his disbelief and the magnitude of his denial of Allah's blessings upon him. It was also said that by "the solitary one" is meant the one whose father is not known, and it was said about al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah that he was an adopted son (du'iya).

﴿And I made for him abundant wealth﴾: i.e., much, or that it increases in growth and increase, one thing after another.

Al-Zajjaj said: wealth not cut off from him. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah was well known for abundance of wealth in its various kinds. It was said that from the produce of his property he obtained a thousand thousand dinars, and it was said four thousand dinars, and it was said one thousand dinars.

﴿And sons present﴾: i.e., and I made for him sons present in Makkah with him, who did not travel and did not need to disperse in search of provision, because of the abundance of their father's wealth.

Al-Dahhak said: They were seven, seven born in Makkah and five born in al-Ta'if.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They were thirteen sons.

Muqatil said: They were seven, all of them men. Three of them became Muslims: Khalid, Hisham and al-Walid ibn al-Walid. After the revelation of this verse, al-Walid continued to decline in his wealth and his children until he died.

It was said that the meaning of "present" (shuhudan) is that when he is mentioned, they are mentioned with him. It was said that they used to attend what he attended and take charge of what he was engaged in.

﴿And I spread for him, spreading﴾: i.e., I extended for him in life, in long life, and in leadership among Quraysh. Tamhid (spreading) among the Arabs means preparation, and from it comes "mahd al-sabi" (the cradle of the child).

Mujahid said: It refers to property, some of it upon some, as a bed is spread.

﴿Then he desires that I should increase﴾: i.e., after all this he desires more increase, because of his great greed and intense covetousness, along with his ingratitude for blessings and his associating partners with Allah.

Al-Hasan said: Then he desires that I should admit him into Paradise. He used to say: If Muhammad is truthful, then Paradise was created only for me.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, restrained and rebuked him, saying: ﴿No!﴾, i.e., I will not increase him.

Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he has been stubborn toward Our signs﴾, i.e., opposing them and disbelieving in what We sent down from them upon Our Messenger. It is said: "anada, ya'nidu" with a kasra, when one opposes the truth and rejects it while knowing it, so he is "anid" and "ani'd." The ani'd is one who deviates from the path and turns away from the right course. From this is the words of al-Harithi:

*When I ride, make me in the middle, for I am old and cannot bear the stubborn.*

Abu Salih said: "'anid" means "distant."

Qatadah said: "jahid" (one who denies).

Muqatil said: "mu'rid" (one who turns away).

﴿I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent﴾: i.e., I will impose upon him a burden of punishment, and it is a parable for the difficult punishment which cannot be borne. It was also said the meaning is that he will be made to climb a mountain of fire. In the speech of the Arabs, "irhaq" means that a person carries a heavy thing.

The clause ﴿Indeed he reflected and determined﴾ gives the reason for the threat mentioned before it. That is, he reflected on the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and on the Qur'an that had been revealed to him, and he determined within himself, that is, he prepared the speech in his mind. The Arabs say "hayya'tu al-shay'" (I prepared the thing) when they mean "qaddartu," and "qaddartu al-shay'" (I determined the thing) when they mean "hayya'tu." This is because, when he heard the Qur'an, he kept reflecting on what to say about it and prepared in his mind what he would say.

So Allah censured him and said: ﴿Then he was killed, how he determined﴾. That is, he was cursed and punished for how he determined, that is, in what manner he determined what he determined of speech. This is like the saying in speech, "I will strike him however he acts," meaning in whatever manner he acts. It has also been said that the meaning is: he was overpowered and defeated, however he determined. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"Your eyes shed tears only so that you may strike,*
*with your two arrows, into the parts of a pierced heart."*

Al-Zuhri said: "He was punished." This is in the form of a curse against him.

The repetition in His saying ﴿Then he was killed, how he determined﴾ is for emphasis and intensification.

﴿Then he looked﴾, that is, by what means he might repel the Qur'an and discredit it, or he reflected on the Qur'an and considered what it is.

﴿Then he frowned﴾, that is, he contracted his face because he did not find a flaw by which to attack the Qur'an. The noun "al-'abs" is the verbal noun of "'abasa" (with a light form), "ya'bisu 'absan wa 'uburran," when one frowns. It has been said that he frowned at the faces of the believers, and it has been said that he frowned at the face of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And scowled﴾, that is, his face became contorted and changed. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"We attacked Tamim at dawn of al-Hifar,*
*with a grey (horse) struck by a dark, scowling one."*

And the saying of another:

*"Her turning away has troubled me, which I saw,*
*and her aversion from my need, and her scowling."*

It has been said that the appearance of frowning on the face comes after the exchange of words, while the appearance of scowling on the face comes before it. The Arabs say "wajh basir" (a scowling face) when it has changed and turned black.

Al-Raghib said: "Al-busr" is hastening evil before its time, like "basara al-rajulu hajatahu," meaning he sought his need out of its proper time.

He said: From this is His saying ﴿frowned and scowled﴾, meaning he displayed frowning before its time and before its moment. The people of Yemen say, "basara al-markab and absara," meaning the ship stood still, neither advancing nor retreating. "Qad ubsirna" means "we have come to scowling."

﴿Then he turned his back and became arrogant﴾, that is, he turned away from the truth, went to his family, and magnified himself against believing.

﴿So he said: This is nothing but magic that is transmitted﴾, that is, he takes it from others and relates it from them.

Magic (al-sihr) is the display of falsehood in the form of truth, or deception, as its explanation was given earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. It is said "athartu al-hadith bi-atharihi" (I relayed the report by its chain) when you mention it from another. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*"What is in it, that you two contended over,*
*is clear to the listener and to the transmitted report."*

﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being﴾, meaning it is the speech of men, not the speech of Allah. This is an emphasis of what precedes it. It will come that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah only said this saying to please his people, after he had acknowledged that it has a sweetness and that it has a radiance, up to the end of his statement.

When he said this saying that Allah related about him, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿I will cast him into Saqar﴾, that is, I will make him enter the Fire. Saqar is one of the names of the Fire and one of the levels of Jahannam. It has been said that this sentence is a substitute for His saying ﴿I will force him to a steep ascent﴾.

Then He (glorified is He) exaggerated in describing the Fire and the severity of its matter, and said: ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾, that is, what will make you know what it is. The Arabs say, "wa-ma adraka ma kadha" (and what will make you know what such-and-such is) when they want to exaggerate its matter, magnify its affair and make its calamity terrifying. The first "ma" is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿what Saqar is﴾ is its predicate.

Then He explained its state, saying: ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾. The clause is resumptive, to explain the state of Saqar and to reveal its description. It has been said that it is in a place of accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element in it is the meaning of magnification, because His saying ﴿and what will make you know what Saqar is﴾ indicates magnification, as if He said: "Magnify Saqar in this state." The first view is better. The object of the two verbs is omitted.

Al-Suddi said: "It leaves for them no flesh and leaves for them no bone."

Ata' said: "It leaves none within it alive, nor leaves it dead." It has also been said that they are two words with one meaning, repeated for emphasis, like your saying "sadda 'anni" and "a'rada 'anni" (he turned away from me and he avoided me).

﴿Scorching to the human being﴾. The majority read ﴿Scorching﴾ with a nominative ending, as the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'). It has been said that it is an adjective of Saqar, and the first is better.

Al-Hasan, 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi, Nasr ibn 'Asim, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with an accusative ending, as a circumstantial clause (hal) or as a specification for the sake of terror. It is said: "laha yaluhu," meaning it appeared; the meaning is that it appears to the human beings.

Al-Hasan said: "Jahannam shows itself to them until they see it directly," like His saying: ﴿And Hell is brought forth for whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿scorching to the human being﴾ is that it changes them and blackens them.
